title: Cache Write Policies
summary: Write-through vs write-back, and the write-allocate decision — how a cache keeps itself consistent with memory on a write.

slides.subTitle: Cache and memory can disagree
slides.markdown:
Reads are simple: fetch a copy, nothing changes. Writes are harder — if the CPU updates a value that lives in cache, memory now holds a **stale** copy unless something propagates the change. **Write policy** decides *when* that propagation happens.

Get this wrong and you get real bugs: a device reading directly from RAM (like a DMA transfer) can see old data if the cache never wrote its update back before the transfer started.

slides.subTitle: Every write goes to memory
slides.markdown:
**Write-through** sends every write to both the cache line and memory immediately. Cache and memory are never out of sync, which makes reasoning about consistency trivial — there's no stale-copy problem to worry about.

The cost is bandwidth: a program that writes the same address a thousand times in a loop still generates a thousand memory writes, even though only the final value ever mattered. This is usually mitigated with a **write buffer** that queues writes so the CPU doesn't stall on each one, but the memory traffic itself is still there.

slides.subTitle: Defer until eviction
slides.markdown:
**Write-back** keeps writes in the cache line only, marking it **dirty**, and defers writing to memory until that line is evicted. A thousand writes to the same address cost one eventual memory write, not a thousand — far better bandwidth use.

This needs a **dirty bit** per line: clean lines can simply be dropped on eviction, but dirty lines must be written back first or the update is lost forever. Most modern CPU caches default to write-back for exactly this bandwidth advantage.

slides.subTitle: Allocate or not?
slides.markdown:
A **write miss** — writing to an address not currently in cache — raises a second, independent question: **write-allocate** fetches the line into cache first, then writes into it (betting the address will be read or written again soon). **No-write-allocate** writes straight to memory and skips loading the line into cache at all.

Write-allocate pays a fetch you might not need again; no-write-allocate skips populating the cache for data that's about to be reused. Neither is universally right — it depends on whether writes to that region tend to repeat.

slides.subTitle: The dirty bit's lifecycle
slides.markdown:
One bit per line is all write-back needs to track.

![A dirty bit's lifecycle — set on write, checked and cleared on eviction](assets/dirty-bit-lifecycle.svg)

On a write, the bit flips to 1. On eviction, the cache checks the bit: 1 means write the line back to memory first; 0 means the line already matches memory and can simply be discarded.

assets.alt: A dirty bit's lifecycle — set on write, checked and cleared on eviction

slides.subTitle: Why they pair the way they do
slides.markdown:
| Pairing | Behavior | Why it's common |
|---|---|---|
| Write-through + no-write-allocate | Writes go straight to memory; a write miss never pulls the line into cache | Simple, consistent, and avoids caching data written once and rarely read |
| Write-back + write-allocate | Writes stay in cache, dirty-marked; a write miss fetches the line first | Maximizes reuse of both the fetched line and the deferred write, matching write-back's bandwidth goal |

**How to decide:** write-through's whole point is simplicity, so pairing it with no-allocate avoids extra cache pollution for data you're not betting on reusing. Write-back's whole point is deferred, batched writes, so pairing it with allocate ensures the line is actually in cache to accumulate those writes.

slides.subTitle: Losing a write on eviction
slides.markdown:
**Wrong belief:** "Evicting a cache line just means overwriting it — the old data doesn't matter since it's still in memory."

**Why it's wrong:** in a write-back cache, a **dirty** line holds the *only* up-to-date copy — memory's copy is stale. Evicting it without writing back first silently discards the update, exactly the bug that appears when firmware forgets to flush dirty lines before a device reads memory directly.

**Correct model:** every eviction must check the dirty bit and write back first if set. "Just overwrite it" is only safe for clean lines.
